Island
i'land
n. (a body of land surrounded by water; in the KJV also isle; rendering Hebrew i, Greek nesos)
From the Saxon igland, water-land; the intrusive s was added later by false association with the unrelated isle, from Latin insula. Hebrew i means a coastland or island, and in the prophets stands for the distant maritime nations.

Biblical Definition

An island in Scripture is a place at the edge of the known world, and the Bible's interest in islands is chiefly that the gospel reaches them. Luke, a careful traveller, names them as they pass: “running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat” (Acts 27:16), and after the wreck, “when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita” (Acts 28:1). On that island a viper fastened on Paul's hand, the islanders changed their minds about him twice, and the father of the chief man was healed — a shipwreck turned into a mission. John writes Revelation from one: “I John… was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Revelation 1:9). A prisoner on a rock in the Aegean received the vision of the throne, which is a permanent comment on where God does his largest work. And the islands appear at the end: “the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places” (Revelation 6:14). The most fixed things men know — mountains and islands, the very definition of permanence to a sailor — are moved. Isaiah had promised long before that the isles should wait for God's law.

Webster 1828 Definition

Land surrounded by water, and in Scripture the edge of the known world. Paul is wrecked on one and heals there; John receives Revelation on one; and at the end every island is moved out of its place.

expand to see more

ISLAND, n. i'land. [Sax. igland, water-land; the s is an intruder from the unrelated isle.] A tract of land surrounded by water.

2. A large mass of floating ice is called an island of ice.

3. ISLE, n. ile. [L. insula.] An island; a tract of land surrounded by water.

4. ISLANDER, n. An inhabitant of an island.

5. In Scripture, the isles, the maritime countries and distant coasts; the isles shall wait for his law, Is. 42.

Key Scripture

Acts 27:16 — "And running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat:"

Acts 28:1 — "And when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita."

Revelation 1:9 — "I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ."

Revelation 6:14 — "And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places."

Modern Corruption

Isolation is treated as exile from usefulness — a believer set aside by circumstance assumed to be out of God's service — when Patmos produced Revelation and a shipwreck produced a mission.

expand to see more

The instinct that God's work happens at centres, in front of crowds, and in seasons of freedom is very hard to shake, and it leaves Christians in confined circumstances concluding that their useful years are over. Scripture's record is otherwise with monotonous regularity. Joseph in a prison, Daniel in a foreign court, Paul in chains writing to Philippi, John on a rock — the confinements are where much of the Bible was produced. John states plainly why he was there: for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. The island was a punishment intended to silence him, and it is the address from which the church received its vision of the throne, the Lamb, and the city.

The principle to recover is Melita. A ship breaks up, a prisoner swims ashore among strangers, and what follows is a fire of sticks, a snake, a healing, and three months of hospitality that ended with the whole island provisioning the voyage. None of it was planned by Paul, and all of it was providence. Christians whose plans have come apart in a storm should read Acts 28 slowly. The Lord had told Paul in Acts 27 that he must be brought before Caesar; getting there involved a wreck, and the wreck was not a detour from the mission but part of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew i is an island or coastland, used in the prophets for the distant maritime nations. Greek nesos is an island; nesion, a small island.

expand to see more

Hebrew i (H339) — an island, a coastland; the isles that shall wait for his law, Isaiah 42:4.

Hebrew choph (H2348) — a coast or haven; often paired with the isles in prophetic geography.

Greek nesos (G3520) — an island; Melita, Patmos, and the islands moved in Revelation 6:14.

Greek nesion (G3519) — a small island; Clauda, under which the ship ran in Acts 27:16.

Greek naugeo (G3489) — to suffer shipwreck; Paul's repeated experience, 2 Corinthians 11:25.

Usage

"Of the wreck that became a mission: they knew that the island was called Melita (Acts 28:1)."

"Of a prisoner given the Revelation: was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God (Revelation 1:9)."

"Of the last dislocation: every mountain and island were moved out of their places (Revelation 6:14)."
